newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan November jobless rate at 2.86 percent.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan November jobless rate at 2.86 percent.

text.p: Taiwan's unemployment rate was at 2.86 percent in November, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said on Monday.
The directorate said November's unemployment rate was at what it regarded as a "normal" level despite official state policy aiming to keep joblessness at 2.0-2.5 percent.
"It is impossible to maintain the jobless rate at the 1.5 percent level as in previous years," said Chao Hung-ching, a directorate section chief.
Taiwan's jobless rate held close to 1.5 percent in 1991-1994 but rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and has pushed above 3.0 percent in August, September and October 1996.

Chao attributed the shift to higher jobless levels to a fundamental change in Taiwan's economy -- a broad move toward service-oriented industries from labour-intensive manufacturing that had engendered the island's dramatic economic development.

Taiwan's unemployment remains low compared to that in the world's developed economies, but the rise above three percent had caused some concern because it coincided with widespread forecasts of a long-awaited economic recovery.
Chao said another important factor was a change in hiring and firing attitudes caused by the increased cost to employers of Taiwan's social insurance system, adopted in March 1995.
The system obliges firms to insure workers' families for health care as well as the workers themselves.
Companies having economic difficulties are quicker to fire workers now because they can save on health insurance premiums as well as salaries and other employee costs, Chao said.
The number of unemployed people in November fell 16,000 to 269,000 from October, while the number of employed rose 65,000 to 9.133 million, the directorate said.
The average unemployment period was 23 weeks, it said.
Unemployment among college graduates was at 3.22 percent in November, down from 3.64 percent in October.
The jobless rate in 1997 should fall to within the target range of 2.0-2.5 percent range as set by the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Developement, Chao said.
"We have no plan to change that projection at the moment," Chao said.
